steps: This video shows task decomposition: why three focused prompts beat one big one. Maya's manager sends her a big request: redesign the new hire onboarding process.
Maya pastes the whole request into Claude as one broad prompt, and gets back a vague three paragraph overview. Even retrying with more detail, it stays shallow.
A colleague spots the problem. That one request hides three distinct deliverables: a process map, training materials and a measurement plan. That means three prompts.
Prompt one asks only for the process map, so Claude's full reasoning goes into that single piece of work, and it returns a process map.
Prompt two asks only for the training materials that support the new process, and Claude returns them as the second deliverable.
Prompt three asks only for the measurement plan, the third distinct deliverable, and Claude returns it, completing the set.

Finally, Maya combines the three specific, well-structured outputs into one final proposal for her manager. When a request hides several deliverables, give each one its own prompt. The full walkthrough is in the Gennoor Claude certification course.
